failure_modes.description: Traffic systems are known to exhibit emergent chaos and non-linear dynamics that make gradient descent fundamentally inappropriate
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic flow research has consistently shown that microscopic traffic behavior follows non-linear dynamics with phase transitions and chaos, making gradient-based optimization methods unstable

failure_modes.description: The assumption that intersections can reliably communicate performance metrics to neighbors is unrealistic
failure_modes.evidence: Real-world traffic systems have communication delays, packet loss, and inconsistent data transmission that would completely disrupt gradient descent calculations

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis fails to account for boundary effects where edge intersections have fewer neighbors
failure_modes.evidence: Edge intersections in any traffic network will have asymmetric neighbor relationships, creating bias in the optimization process that would lead to systematically poor performance at network boundaries

failure_modes.description: The system would exhibit persistent oscillations even under steady-state conditions
failure_modes.evidence: Gradient descent with delayed feedback (inevitable in real traffic systems) creates positive feedback loops that cause oscillations - this is a fundamental limitation of distributed control with communication delays

failure_modes.description: Similar distributed approaches have already been tried and failed
failure_modes.evidence: Previous attempts at distributed traffic signal optimization (e.g., PRODYN, OPAC) all required significant central coordination and failed when truly decentralized

failure_modes.description: Local optimization objectives conflict with global traffic efficiency
failure_modes.evidence: Minimizing local queue lengths often creates phantom jams and reduces overall throughput - this is a well-documented phenomenon in traffic engineering
